title: One slow SD card failed two releases without an error
duration: about a day and a half of a slowing node; two releases rolled back, the old version served throughout
what: One Pi's SD card, from 2016, slowed down without reporting a single error: a synced write went from 8-17 ms to 700-2400 ms. Pods on that node took 3-5 minutes to start. Two releases of this page went out as canaries, the new copy landed on that Pi, didn't get ready within the 5 minutes allowed, and Flagger rolled both back. Visitors kept getting the old version. The alert meant to catch a slowing card wanted a week of history and had three days, so nothing fired.
fix: The card was replaced with a clone: same partition table and IDs, so nothing on the node had to change. New alerts: a card whose daily median write is over 100 ms, an hour of high iowait, and slow pod starts. Backtested on this data, the first would have fired hours before the first failed release. The Cluster tab now shows each card's age, how many times it has been written over, and its write time.
lesson: A failed canary is a symptom, not a cause. Hardware that slows down instead of breaking passes every health check.

title: This page showed 95-minute-old results after a game day
duration: about 95 minutes, 07:05 to 08:40 UTC: the page answered, its check results stopped at 07:05
what: I crashed one of the four Pis on purpose, to test that DNS keeps working with the second DNS server I had added that morning. DNS passed. The Pi didn't: when it came back, its old, slow SD card was saturated, and the container runtime couldn't start anything in time. Every pod on it stayed in an error state while the node reported itself healthy, so Kubernetes moved nothing away. The next run of the status checker was scheduled there and hung, and the checker never runs twice at once, so no further check ran. The sites themselves kept answering from their other copies: not one failed request. The stale-data alert fired; nothing told me why, because the service that reports pod states ran on the same Pi.
fix: Moving everything off that Pi and rebooting it cleared it, and its card was fast again afterwards. A new alert now reads the node's own count of failed container starts, which doesn't depend on any pod; the pod-state service no longer runs on the Pi with the slow card; and the game-day script now calls a run that never recovers a failure, instead of a pass.
lesson: A node can be Ready and useless at the same time. Kubernetes moves pods off a node that stops reporting, not off one that reports fine and can't do anything.

title: The cluster dashboard ran without its backend for four hours
duration: about 4 hours, 10:55 to 14:44 UTC: the dashboard page loaded, its data didn't
what: The day before, the public namespaces got default-deny network policies, mapped from the traffic I could see. The dashboard's backend also keeps its users and sessions in MongoDB Atlas, and that connection wasn't on the list. Nothing failed at first: the running pods kept their open connections. The next morning a rebuilt image started new pods, they couldn't reach Atlas, and they crash-looped. The page itself still answered, so it looked up; every request for data got a 502. The alerts fired, as a set of pod and traffic alerts, while I wasn't looking.
fix: The backend may now reach Atlas on its port, outside the private address ranges. The pods started at once.
lesson: A network policy is only tested when connections are new. Restart the pods after applying one, or the old connections hide what's missing.

title: A cached 404 left this page without its script
duration: about 15 minutes, 06:15 to 06:30 UTC, for visitors served by Cloudflare's London edge
what: A new version of this page went out as a canary, so for a few minutes the old and the new version served side by side. A visitor got the new index.html from one and asked the other for the new script, which the old version did not have, so it answered 404. Cloudflare kept that 404 for 4 hours. Once the new version was promoted, every visitor to that edge got a page whose script could not load. I noticed it while checking the release, not from an alert: the status checks only ask for the page itself, which was fine.
fix: Error answers from this page now carry Cache-Control: no-store, so no cache keeps them. The fix went out as the next release, whose script has a new name, so the cached 404 was no longer asked for and nothing had to be purged by hand.
lesson: A canary release mixes two versions in one visit, and a cache in front can turn a moment of that into hours. Errors should never be cacheable.

title: Three days of node backups that could not be opened
duration: found before any of them was needed
what: Before each OS upgrade, the upgrade script saved every Pi's configuration to another machine. While writing a runbook for replacing a Pi's SD card, I opened one of these backups for the first time: it broke off after a few hundred of its 3,100 files. So did all seven. The script sent the compressed stream through a helper that hides the Pi's login banner, a text filter that quietly cut bytes out of binary data. Every command exited fine and the files had plausible sizes, so nothing looked wrong.
fix: Backups now bypass that helper, and the receiving machine reads each one to the end and looks for a known file before accepting it; otherwise the upgrade stops. The next morning that check caught a backup cut short by a network drop.
lesson: A backup you have never restored from is a hope. The cluster's own database backups were safe, because they are restore-tested every week; these were not.

title: Switching a Pi to 64-bit removed its ssh server
duration: the Pi was out of rotation for 2.5 hours instead of 30 minutes
what: I switched each Pi's operating system from 32-bit to 64-bit in place, rehearsed first on a copy of the system. On the first real Pi, the 32-bit systemd refused to be replaced while it was running, something the copy could not reproduce. The script's automatic repair let the package manager resolve it, and it did so by removing about 100 packages, the ssh server and the network manager among them. A final check noticed and stopped before the reboot, so the Pi stayed up but unreachable over ssh, with no traffic on it.
fix: Repaired from inside Kubernetes with a debug pod on the node, reinstalling the missing packages. systemd now switches on its own first, every risky step is simulated and refused if it would remove anything it should not, and the rehearsal looks like a running system. The other three Pis then switched in one go each, with no failed requests.
lesson: A rehearsal only proves what it reproduces, and an automatic repair needs a limit checked before it acts.

title: Game day: seven tries to survive a node that dies
duration: a few failed requests per run; the worst run, about 45 seconds of 502s
what: I made one Pi fail on purpose: stop k3s and kill every container on it, no warning, and probe every site once a second from the VPS while it stays dead for three minutes. Every run failed a little differently, each time one layer further out. First, the other nodes kept forwarding part of the traffic to the dead node's Kong gateway until Kubernetes noticed, about a minute later. Then Kong, and after that the VPS's nginx, waited 60 seconds on kept-alive connections into the dead node, which never answer and never reset. The fifth run was the worst, and that one was my fault: to cut the waiting I had shortened nginx's connect timeout to one second, so it marked all four nodes as failed within seconds and returned 502 to everyone for about 45 seconds.
fix: A packet capture on a healthy node finally showed the root cause: the VPS's connections arrived and were never answered. Port 80 on each node goes through a small k3s load-balancer pod, and Kubernetes treats traffic coming from a pod as internal and spreads it across every node's gateway, the dead one included, even with "local traffic only" set. The VPS now connects to Kong's node port directly, where each node only uses its own gateway. With that, plus one Kong gateway per node, shorter timeouts inside Kong and no connection reuse from the VPS, the seventh run passed: three minutes with a dead node, zero failed requests.
lesson: A setting that says "local only" may not cover the path your traffic actually takes; it took a packet capture, not a config read, to see it. And a fix for slow failover can turn into an outage of its own: give up too quickly and every node looks dead.

title: My own change to the cluster's way in took every site down for 30 seconds
duration: about 32 seconds, all sites; then about 50 seconds of slow requests
what: To fix the node-crash problem above, I changed Kong's gateway from two replicas to one on every node. Helm created the new set and removed the old one in the same step, before any new pod was ready, so for about 32 seconds there was no gateway at all and every site returned 502. The follow-up setting change made k3s restart its load-balancer pods on all four nodes within eight seconds, and requests stalled for another 50 seconds or so.
fix: Nothing to roll back; both changes finished on their own and were what I wanted, just not how they rolled out.
lesson: For anything on the way in, bring the new path up next to the old one first and only then remove the old one. Two steps that each look safe are not a plan if one of them replaces the thing that serves the traffic.

title: Upgrading one Pi took the sites down for 75 seconds
what: While patching the control-plane Pi, I drained it first, which moves its pods to the other nodes. Every app ran as a single replica with nothing saying "keep one running", so while each pod restarted somewhere else there was nothing left to serve the sites. The VPS had a second weak spot: it sent all cluster traffic to that one Pi only.
fix: Two replicas of everything public, on different Pis, with a disruption budget so a drain always leaves one running; a 10-second grace period so a pod keeps serving while Kong takes it out of rotation; and the VPS now sends traffic to all four Pis. The next drain of the same node lost no requests.
lesson: Automatic reboots (kured) were the next step, so this had to be fixed first: otherwise every night's patching would have been a small outage.

title: k3s upgrade 1.30 to 1.37: a short outage and an alert storm
what: I upgraded the cluster seven Kubernetes versions in a row, one node at a time. While the control plane restarted, the two sites served from the cluster returned 502 for about two minutes. Twice the status checker's own node restarted under it, and it recorded every site as down, including the ones on other servers. Those fake failures set off the SLO alerts for all eight services at once. That notification was too big for ntfy, which rejected it, and the rejection crashed Alertmanager through a bug in version 0.27. It restarted for about 40 minutes, re-sending the same alerts each time.
fix: Silenced the false alerts, upgraded Alertmanager to 0.28.1 (which has the fix), and capped how many alerts go into one notification.
lesson: The checker now skips a run in which no site answered at all, because that is its own network, not eight outages. Upgrades now silence only the alerts a rolling restart is expected to cause; the SLO alerts stay live.

title: Mail server certificate would have expired in December
what: While setting up certificate expiry monitoring, I listed the certificates on the VPS. Three Let's Encrypt certificates, including the mail server's, were due to expire in mid-December, and nothing was going to renew them: the renewal timer had been enabled but never started. There was a second problem behind it: even after a renewal, the mail server would have kept serving the old certificate, because nothing told it to reload.
fix: Started the renewal timer, tested the renewal against Let's Encrypt's staging environment, and added a hook that reloads the mail server after a renewal.
lesson: Every public certificate, the mail ports and the cluster's own certificates are now probed hourly, with an alert 14 days before expiry.

title: Critical alerts that had been firing for months
what: Before sending alerts to my phone I checked what was already firing, and found three critical "component down" alerts that had been on the whole time. k3s runs the scheduler, controller-manager and kube-proxy inside its one process, so the default monitoring stack never found them. Two Services left behind by earlier monitoring installs also made Prometheus scrape every kubelet three times, which broke some of its rules.
fix: Turned off the monitors k3s has no targets for and deleted the leftover Services, before anything was routed to a phone.
lesson: Clean up the alert noise first. Paging on top of alerts that are always on teaches you to ignore the pager.

title: One failed check on RunGuard, cause unknown
what: The checker marked RunGuard down once, and the next check was fine again. By the time I looked, the Job logs were gone, and the checker had only stored "down", not why. RunGuard's own logs and nginx show no restart or error, so the cause can't be found any more.
fix: Nothing to fix by then. While looking, I did find that RunGuard deploys stopped the service for the whole binary upload; they now upload first and only restart for the swap.
lesson: The checker now stores the reason with every failed check (timeout, connection error or HTTP status), and you can see it by hovering over a red bar. The next one won't be a mystery.

title: All sites on the cluster down for a few minutes
what: I applied the Gateway manifest from the repo to the live cluster. That file is a template for people running their own copy, with a placeholder where the Gateway class name goes, and I applied it with the placeholder still in. Kong dropped the shared Gateway, and every public hostname on the cluster stopped answering.
fix: Re-applied the manifest with the real class name.
lesson: Hand-applied manifests are a risk. Moving the cluster to GitOps, so the live state always comes from reviewed config, is on the list.

title: Admin certificate expired, and nothing noticed
what: The client certificate my laptop uses to manage the cluster expired. Nothing watched it, so I only found out in November when kubectl stopped working. The cluster itself kept running.
fix: Worked through SSH on the control-plane node in the meantime, then issued a new kubeconfig.
lesson: Certificate expiry monitoring, for both the public TLS certificates and the cluster's own, is the next item on the list.
